blurb: How we test AI — exams, leaderboards, AI graders and safety checks — and why every score deserves a second look.

steps.p: A benchmark is a set of questions with known answers that every model sits. Scores make models easy to compare.
steps.analogy: Like a standardised school exam: handy for comparing, but not the whole story about a student.

steps.p: Benchmarks get posted online, and online text ends up in training data. A model may have seen the questions — called contamination.

items: Score looks better than real skill

steps.p: Once top models score near 100%, a test can't separate them any more — it's saturated.
Benchmarks have wrong answer keys and ambiguous questions too. Near the top, models may be marked wrong for being right.
A high general score says little about your specific job. The best check is a handful of your own real examples.

cards.q: MMLU, long a headline benchmark, tests…
cards.why: Broad knowledge. About 16,000 questions from school to professional level, from law to physics. Top models now score around 90%.

cards.statement: A model with a high MMLU score is guaranteed to do well on your specific task.
cards.why: False. Knowing facts across 57 subjects doesn't prove it can write your reports or fix your code. Test on your own examples.

cards.title: A 2024 audit estimated about 6.5% of MMLU's questions contain errors — over half of them in its virology section.
cards.detail: The "Are We Done with MMLU?" study found wrong answer keys, unclear questions and multiple correct options.

cards.q: One way to detect that a model has seen test questions before is to…
options: Reword the questions and see whether the score drops sharply
Ask the model if it cheated
cards.hint: Memory depends on exact wording; understanding doesn't.
cards.why: Reword and compare. A model that understands handles fresh wording; one that memorised the originals stumbles.

cards.statement: Different labs always measure the same benchmark in the same way.
cards.why: False. Prompt wording, number of examples and how answers are extracted all vary — and can shift scores by several points.

steps.p: You ask a question and get answers from two anonymous chatbots side by side. You vote for the better one.

visual.caption: Vote first, then the names are revealed.

steps.p: Names are only shown after the vote so people judge the answer, not the logo.
Votes feed an Elo-style rating: beat a stronger model and you gain lots of points; beat a weaker one and you gain few.
People tend to prefer longer, nicely formatted, confident answers — even when they're not more correct.
Critics argue some labs test many private versions and publish only the best score, inflating rankings.

cards.q: Why are models kept anonymous until after the vote?
options: So people vote on answer quality, not brand
cards.why: No brand bias. If you knew which was which, your opinion of the company could sway your vote.

cards.statement: Arena rankings can be swayed by style, such as longer answers and heavy formatting.
cards.why: True. Bullet points and length look thorough. The arena now offers rankings with style effects adjusted out.

cards.q: In an Elo-style system, beating a much higher-rated opponent earns…
options: More points, because the upset was unlikely
cards.why: More points. Ratings move most when results are surprising. An expected win barely changes anything.

cards.title: A 2025 paper, "The Leaderboard Illusion", alleged some labs privately tested many versions on the arena and published only the best.
cards.detail: Picking the top score from many private tries inflates rankings. The arena disputed parts of the analysis, but the debate highlighted how leaderboards can be gamed.

cards.statement: Arena-style voting measures factual accuracy precisely.
cards.why: False. Voters often can't check facts. It measures which answers people prefer, which overlaps with accuracy but isn't the same.

steps.p: Instead of people, a strong model reads answers and scores them, or picks the better of two. This is called LLM-as-a-judge.
It can mark thousands of answers in minutes for a fraction of what people would cost.
Judges favour the first answer shown, longer answers, and answers written in their own style.
Run each comparison twice with the order swapped, and only count a win if it holds both times.
Give the judge specific criteria and a reference answer. Vague questions like "which is better?" get vague marking.
steps.analogy: A teacher with a marking scheme grades more fairly than one going on gut feel.

cards.q: To correct a judge's habit of favouring whichever answer comes first, you can…
options: Run the comparison twice with the order swapped and combine the results
Always put the best answer first
Ask the judge to be fair
cards.why: Swap and repeat. If an answer wins in both positions, the win is real, not a side effect of order.

cards.statement: AI judges tend to prefer answers written by themselves.
cards.why: True. Studies have found self-preference: a model rates its own style higher. Using a different model as judge helps.

cards.title: Strong AI judges agreed with human experts about as often as humans agreed with each other.
cards.detail: A 2023 study (MT-Bench) found GPT-4's judgements matched human preferences over 80% of the time — similar to human-to-human agreement.

cards.q: What most improves an AI judge's reliability?
options: Specific criteria plus a reference answer to compare against
cards.why: A marking scheme. Clear criteria and a model answer turn a gut feeling into a check.

cards.title: Build a tiny test for your own use
cards.body: Write 5 real questions from your life or work, with what a great answer looks like. Run any new AI tool through them.
cards.challenge: Write down three questions you often ask AI and note what a perfect answer would include.

steps.p: Agent tests give a goal in a realistic setting — a computer, a website, a codebase — and check the end result.
Agents are partly random. The same task can succeed once and fail the next, so each is run several times.

visual.caption: 5 runs of one task: a 60% success rate, not "it works".

steps.p: Labs and government institutes check whether models could meaningfully help with things like cyberattacks or bioweapons.
Policies like Anthropic's tie stronger protections to capability levels: cross a line in testing, and extra safeguards are required.
A model failing once might succeed with better prompting or tools. Testers try hard to bring out the most capability.
steps.analogy: One failed lock-pick attempt doesn't prove the lock is unpickable.

cards.statement: OSWorld tests agents on real desktop apps inside a virtual computer.
cards.why: True. Agents must complete tasks like editing spreadsheets across real operating systems, graded automatically on the result.

cards.q: Why should agent tests be run many times per task?
options: Agents are partly random, so one run can be lucky or unlucky
Because the first run never counts
cards.why: Randomness. One success might be a fluke. Several runs give an honest success rate.

cards.title: US and UK government AI safety institutes have tested frontier models before release.
cards.detail: In late 2024 they jointly published pre-release tests of models including an upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet and OpenAI's o1, covering cyber, biology and software skills.

cards.statement: If a model fails a dangerous-capability test once, it definitely lacks that capability.
cards.why: False. Better prompts, tools or more attempts might succeed. That's why testers try hard to bring out a model's full ability.

cards.q: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy links safety measures to…
options: Capability thresholds a model is tested against
cards.why: Capability thresholds. The more dangerous what a model can do, the stronger the required security and safeguards.
